transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-30
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Priya Natarajan (Redwood SE), Liam Ortiz (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Crestline Head of Data), Mark Delaney (Platform Lead), Sofia Alvarez (Security), Tom Reed (Director of Product)

Auto-generated summary: POC scoping for support summarization and policy extraction workloads. Focus on QPS/concurrency, token distributions, acceptable latency and cost envelope, security checklist and timeline.

Topics:
- Current stack and constraints
- QPS and concurrency targets
- Input/output token distributions and payload examples
- Latency targets (p50/p95) and quality thresholds
- Benchmarks: env, metrics, duration
- Pilot timelines and success criteria

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Hayes: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick intro from our side, i'm jordan, i'll own the pilot and pricing. priya and liam from our engineering side will handle benchmarks.
[00:12] Aisha Khan: thanks jordan. aisha here. to kick off, our team wants to validate a model for support ticket summarization and extracting policy sections for audit. primary concern is latency under load and predictable cost.
[00:28] Priya Natarajan: got it. can you give us a baseline today? qps, concurrency, average and peak payload sizes, that sort of thing.
[00:35] Mark Delaney: sure. today we handle about 18 qps average across our inbound support endpoints, peak spikes to about 120 qps during morning batch retries. concurrency per worker is around 10 to 30. most calls are single-turn but some chains call into policy extraction so they hit models twice in series.
[00:51] Tom Reed: to add, typical session is two requests max. first a summarization of a multi-paragraph ticket, then a policy match call which is shorter.
[01:02] Jordan Hayes: ok that's helpful. what's your typical input size for the summarize request?
[01:07] Aisha Khan: mean input around 600 tokens, median closer to 420, tail up to 2k for long tickets. output target for summary is 80-150 tokens. for policy extraction the input is ~200-400 tokens with outputs around 40-80 tokens.
[01:26] Priya Natarajan: great, that distribution matters for batching and KV cache behavior. for modeling we'll assume a bimodal distribution \u2014 long docs for summarization and short for policy.
[01:36] Liam Ortiz: do you have a sample set you can share? even a 1% anonymized sample helps us create realistic benchmarks.
[01:43] Aisha Khan: yes, we'll provide a sanitized CSV. working on redacting pII but can get an example by next week.
[01:50] Mark Delaney: one more thing \u2014 SLA preference. we care about p95 under 2.5s for the summarization in the interactive UI, ideally p50 around 500-800ms. p95 for policy extraction should be under 1.2s.
[02:03] Priya Natarajan: that's pretty tight at scale. to confirm, p95 measured from request arrival to complete token stream end?
[02:10] Sofia Alvarez: yes, from the front-end call. also encryption at rest + KMS integration is non-negotiable for logs and artifacts.
[02:20] Jordan Hayes: noted. for the pilot we'll propose two runs: hosted API baseline and a dedicated capacity run. that will show tradeoffs in latency and cost.
[02:28] Tom Reed: timeline-wise, we want to decide on vendor by mid-november to start migration early next year. pilot ideally in october.
[02:36] Jordan Hayes: timeline works \u2014 week of 10/12 for benchmarking was our suggestion earlier.

[02:45] Priya Natarajan: digging into traffic modeling: you said average 18 qps and peaks to 120. do you expect sustained peaks or short bursts?
[02:55] Mark Delaney: mostly short bursts, 5-15 minutes during retries and morning catchups, but we have some tenants with heavy bot-driven traffic that can sustain 20-30 qps for several hours.
[03:07] Priya Natarajan: ok we'll model both burst and sustained scenarios. for sizing we need target concurrency. if a single host keeps 32 concurrent streams we can estimate how many hosts for your p95 SLO.
[03:18] Aisha Khan: our infra team prefers to keep latency under 2s for customer-facing flows, willing to accept higher cost for those routes. backend batch jobs can be lower priority and tolerate higher latency.
[03:29] Liam Ortiz: helpful distinction. we'll separate routes in the benchmark: interactive vs background.

[03:40] Jordan Hayes: what's your cost target or constraints? ballpark monthly budget for inference?
[03:44] Tom Reed: we don't have a precise number but we'd like to keep incremental cost under $20k/mo for the pilot scale (production small cohort). main ask is predictable unit cost per 1k tokens.
[03:55] Priya Natarajan: we'll include per-token cost estimates for hosted and dedicated, and show projection for your QPS and token mix. remember that long inputs skew unit cost because of encoder/decoder costs.

[04:05] Mark Delaney: curious about quantization and model variants. do you support 8-bit or 4-bit and does that affect latency significantly?
[04:12] Liam Ortiz: yes we have quantized runtime options; 8-bit usually gives modest throughput gains with minor quality differences, 4-bit can reduce mem and cost more but depends on the model. we'll run quality checks in the POC to ensure extraction fidelity.
[04:24] Aisha Khan: happy to trade a small quality delta for cost savings as long as our audit pass rates for policy extraction stay >95%.

[04:33] Priya Natarajan: noted. can you state success criteria explicitly for this pilot?
[04:38] Tom Reed: success is three-fold: 1) p95 latency for interactive summarization <2.5s under expected peak load, 2) policy extraction precision/recall within 2% of current baseline, 3) predictable cost projection with monthly incremental cost < $20k at pilot scale.
[04:55] Jordan Hayes: good. we'll codify those into the SOW and measurement harness.

[05:02] Mark Delaney: what environment will benchmarks run in? cloud region constraints? we are in AWS us-east-1 primarily.
[05:09] Priya Natarajan: we can run both in us-east-1 hosted endpoints and a dedicated pool provisioned in your VPC if you want to test the private network stack. dedicated in your VPC will show the most realistic latencies and network egress patterns.
[05:22] Sofia Alvarez: VPC peering and customer-managed KMS are required for sensitive data. can you support HSM-backed keys?
[05:29] Liam Ortiz: yes we integrate with KMS/HSM via standard customer-managed key rotation; we'll send the security pack.

[05:37] Jordan Hayes: regarding metrics, we'll capture p50/p90/p95 latency, tokens in/out, cost per 1k tokens, throughput (qps), concurrency, error rate, and memory utilization per host. any additions?
[05:50] Aisha Khan: also capture cold-start events and model switch fallbacks; those matter for our SLAs.
[05:55] Priya Natarajan: good call \u2014 we'll instrument fallbacks and routing changes.

[06:02] Tom Reed: for the benchmark plan, how long will each run be? continuous run for 1-2 hours?
[06:07] Priya Natarajan: standard practice is a warmup + 1-hour steady-state run for each scenario, with a 2-hour run for burst scenarios to capture transient behavior.
[06:16] Jordan Hayes: we'll also run synthetic traces using your traffic CSV and a few recorded real sessions to measure token distribution performance.

[06:27] Aisha Khan: about model choice \u2014 are you proposing a single model or fallbacks across a model family?
[06:33] Liam Ortiz: we'll start with a curated open model we've validated (redwood-verified profile), and one cheaper quantized variant for cost comparison. automatic fallback policy can route to a cheaper model if latency/capacity thresholds are hit.
[06:47] Mark Delaney: fallback sounds useful but we need to ensure output consistency; for policy extraction we can't have drift.
[06:54] Priya Natarajan: for extraction-critical paths we'll disable fallbacks; for summaries we can allow fallback with a quality monitor.

[07:02] Jordan Hayes: let's walk through a sample calculation for capacity. say interactive route gets steady 25 qps, average input 600 tokens, output 120 tokens. that's roughly 25 * (600+120) = 18k tokens/sec? hold on math.
[07:16] Priya Natarajan: small correction \u2014 25 requests/sec * (720 tokens/request) = 18,000 tokens/sec, yes. multiply by 60 for per-minute. downstream cost and throughput depend on tokens/sec and model throughput tokens/s per host.
[07:28] Liam Ortiz: if a host can sustain 40k tokens/sec with batching, you'd need 1 host for that route, but latency SLO and real-world inefficiencies mean we usually add headroom ~30-50%.
[07:40] Mark Delaney: can you explain continuous batching and how that affects latency? we've seen batch optimizations increase throughput but spike tail latency.
[07:47] Priya Natarajan: continuous batching collects requests across a small window (tens of ms) and executes them together. it improves throughput but can add minimal queuing; with smart routing and per-route configs we can keep p95 within SLO. we'll tune batching windows for interactive flows.

[08:05] Aisha Khan: what about KV cache behavior for policy extraction when users hit similar docs?
[08:10] Liam Ortiz: KV cache helps if you have repeated prefixes across sessions; for single-turn summarization its benefit is limited, but for chained calls where the same document is accessed KV cache can cut compute. we'll instrument cache hit rates in the benchmark.

[08:20] Tom Reed: any constraints on request size or streaming for our UI? we plan to stream tokens to the client.
[08:25] Priya Natarajan: streaming is supported. streaming adds some network overhead but improves perceived latency. p95 measured to final token will include streaming time; we'll report both time-to-first-token and time-to-last-token.

[08:40] Jordan Hayes: switching to security briefly \u2014 priya will share SOC 2 summary and how we log audits. sofia, anything else from compliance?
[08:48] Sofia Alvarez: audit logging retention window question: we need 2 years, can that be provisioned?
[08:53] Priya Natarajan: yes, with enterprise add-on we can provide longer retention or export to your S3 with lifecycle policies.

[09:00] Mark Delaney: on data residency, everything must remain in us-east-1 for the pilot.
[09:04] Jordan Hayes: that's fine, we'll scope region-specific hosts.

[09:10] Aisha Khan: the team also wants a smoke test harness we can run internally to validate responses against our eval set.
[09:16] Priya Natarajan: we'll provide a small harness and the eval runner; you can plug in your tests to measure precision/recall passes.

[09:24] Tom Reed: regarding observability, do you provide per-route breakdowns and token level cost?
[09:29] Liam Ortiz: yes, per-route dashboards, token-level cost and tracing to link requests to downstream errors.

[09:36] Jordan Hayes: ok let's recap success criteria and deliverables. success criteria: p95 under 2.5s for interactive summarization under peak scenario, policy extraction accuracy within 2% of baseline, monthly incremental cost < $20k for pilot scale. deliverables: SOW + pricing, benchmark plan, security pack, sanitized traffic CSV, scheduled benchmark window.
[09:57] Aisha Khan: that aligns with our expectations. next, schedule \u2014 can you send SOW by friday?
[10:02] Jordan Hayes: yes we'll send initial SOW by friday 2026-10-02.

[10:10] Priya Natarajan: any other technical concerns?
[10:13] Mark Delaney: fallback handling and cache invalidation logic; we'll want a short doc describing how Redwood's routing and cache TTLs behave.
[10:21] Liam Ortiz: we'll include that in the technical appendix.

[10:27] Sofia Alvarez: last question \u2014 encryption in transit and at rest, can we mandate TLS 1.3 and customer-managed KMS?
[10:33] Priya Natarajan: yes TLS 1.3 supported and CMK integration is standard for private deployments. we'll include key rotation and HSM notes.

[10:40] Tom Reed: thanks all. we're comfortable proceeding with the pilot as outlined.
[10:44] Jordan Hayes: great. to confirm action items: jordan send SOW, priya prepare benchmark plan, aisha share traffic csv, sofia share compliance checklist.
[10:54] Aisha Khan: will do.
[11:00] Jordan Hayes: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email.
[51:55] (call end)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings: 'KV cache' sometimes transcribed as 'KV cash', 'VPC' pronounced 'V-P-C', some proper nouns slightly off.
